lesson.title: The Fetch Execute Cycle: How a CPU Actually Runs a Program
lesson.summary: Explains the fetch, decode, execute cycle by which a CPU processes instructions one at a time, and how the memory hierarchy of registers, cache, and RAM affects how quickly a program runs.
lesson.body:
The previous section introduced the CPU and RAM as two of the core physical components of a computer, but it left an important question unanswered: how does a CPU actually turn a stream of stored instructions into a running program? The answer is a repeating process called the fetch, decode, execute cycle, sometimes just called the fetch execute cycle, which runs continuously, billions of times per second on a modern processor, for as long as the computer is powered on.

The cycle begins with fetch: the CPU looks at a special internal register called the program counter, which holds the memory address of the next instruction to run, retrieves the instruction stored at that address from RAM, and loads it into the CPU. Next comes decode: the CPU examines that instruction and determines what operation it represents, for example, whether it is an instruction to add two numbers, compare two values, or move data from one location to another. Finally comes execute: the CPU actually carries out that operation, using a component called the arithmetic logic unit for math and comparisons, and the program counter is updated to point at the next instruction, so the entire cycle can repeat.

This cycle explains, at the hardware level, exactly what is happening when a Python statement like total = total + 5 runs. Although this looks like one line of code, by the time it reaches the CPU it has been translated into several individual machine instructions: one to fetch the current value of total from memory, one to add 5 to it using the arithmetic logic unit, and one to store the new result back into memory. Each of these smaller instructions goes through its own complete fetch, decode, execute cycle, one after another, even though from the programmer's point of view it appeared as a single, instantaneous step.

Speed in this cycle depends heavily on where data is stored, which is why computers use a memory hierarchy rather than one single kind of memory. Registers, small storage locations built directly into the CPU, are the fastest to access but can only hold a tiny amount of data, often just a single value each. Cache memory sits just outside the CPU and holds slightly more data, still very fast but not as fast as registers. Main memory, the RAM discussed in the previous section, holds far more data than cache but takes noticeably longer for the CPU to reach. Secondary storage, like a solid state drive, holds the most data of all but is slower still, which is exactly why running programs must first be loaded from storage into RAM.

This hierarchy exists because faster memory is significantly more expensive to build per byte than slower memory, so computers use a small amount of very fast memory alongside larger amounts of progressively slower memory, and rely on the CPU keeping frequently used data as close as possible, in registers or cache, to minimize wasted time. Every abstraction covered earlier in this course, a Python list, a function call, a for loop, ultimately reduces to millions of fetch, decode, execute cycles moving data through this hierarchy, which is a genuinely remarkable fact: the high level, readable code you write is, underneath, implemented entirely in terms of this simple, repeating mechanical process.
